diff.text: public static bool TryParseAutolink(StringLineGroup text, out string link, out bool isEmail)
// An absolute URI, for these purposes, consists of a scheme followed by a colon (:)
// followed by zero or more characters other than ASCII whitespace and control characters, <, and >.
// If the URI includes these characters, they must be percent-encoded (e.g. %20 for a space).
// a scheme is any sequence of 2–32 characters
// and followed by any combination of ASCII letters, digits, or the symbols plus (”+”), period (”.”), or hyphen (”-”).
// An email address, for these purposes, is anything that matches the non-normative regex from the HTML5 spec:

reasons.detail: Off-by-one scheme length rejects valid 2-char schemes and 32-char schemes, and email domain validation is broken: pc is never updated and hasMinus is not cleared on alphanumeric, so domain checks for consecutive dots/trailing hyphen fail.

diff.text: // We may have an email char?

reasons.detail: Off-by-one rejects valid 2-char schemes: check `builder.Length <= 2` before colon incorrectly fails when length==2, but spec allows 2-32 char schemes (e.g. `ab:...` should parse).

diff.text: // Chars valid for both scheme and email
// If this is not a special char valid also for url scheme, then we have an email

reasons.detail: Minimum scheme length check uses builder.Length <=2 instead of <2 (or <=1), so valid 2-character schemes (spec says 2–32 chars) are incorrectly rejected, and the 32-char max check is skipped when state==0 allowing over-long schemes to pass.

diff.text: // a scheme is any sequence of 2–32 characters

reasons.detail: Off-by-one rejects valid 2-char schemes: `builder.Length <= 2` returns false for length 2, but spec requires 2–32 chars, so check should be `<2` or `<=1`; e.g. `<ab:...>` would be incorrectly rejected.
Logic-heavy change in source file; Spark Open rated it 10%.

Domain hyphen tracking never clears hasMinus on alphanumeric (assignment only on '-' branch due to || short-circuit), so any email with a hyphen not at end incorrectly fails the final hasMinus check, and pc is never updated so '.-' labels are not rejected.

diff.text: // An absolute URI, for these purposes, consists of a scheme followed by a colon (:)
// followed by zero or more characters other than ASCII whitespace and control characters, <, and >.
// If the URI includes these characters, they must be percent-encoded (e.g. %20 for a space).

reasons.detail: pc variable is never updated in email domain loop so checks for consecutive dots or dot after hyphen (pc=='.'||pc=='-') never trigger, causing invalid emails like a@b..c or a@b-.com to be incorrectly accepted as autolinks.

diff.text: /// Truncate a string to a fixed length while preserving whole words.
/// If the truncation point falls in the middle of a word,
/// that word is dropped entirely and the delimiter is attached.
/// For left-truncation, if no complete word fits in the allowed space,
public string? Truncate(string? value, int length, string? truncationString, TruncateFrom truncateFrom = TruncateFrom.Right)
// For this scenario we expect a single-character delimiter.
// If truncation string is null, treat it as empty.
// If the delimiter itself is longer than the allowed length, fall back to a basic substring.

reasons.detail: Left truncation returns minimal fitting suffix not maximal: it scans from the end and breaks on first whitespace where suffix fits, so with allowed=10 and value='hello world test' it returns '...test' instead of '...world test' which still fits.

diff.text: // If truncation string is null, treat it as empty.
// If the delimiter itself is longer than the allowed length, fall back to a basic substring.
// If the whole string fits, return it.
static string TruncateFromLeft(string value, int length, string truncationString)
// For left truncation, the final output is: delimiter + substring.
// Determine how many characters (after the delimiter) are allowed.
// We'll scan backward from the end of the string for a whitespace boundary
// such that the substring (after trimming) is no longer than allowedContentLength.

reasons.detail: TruncateFromLeft scans backward and breaks on first whitespace that fits, so it returns only the last word instead of the longest word-bounded suffix that fits in allowedContentLength, truncating too aggressively.

diff.text: // We'll scan backward from the end of the string for a whitespace boundary
// such that the substring (after trimming) is no longer than allowedContentLength.
// If the candidate word is too long (i.e. would be partial) or empty, return just the delimiter.
static string TruncateFromRight(string value, int length, string truncationString)

reasons.detail: TruncateFromLeft scans backwards and breaks on the first whitespace where candidate fits, so it returns the shortest suffix that fits (e.g. just 'bar') instead of the longest fitting suffix ('foo bar'), dropping words that should be kept.

diff.text: /// Truncate a string to a fixed number of letters or digits,
/// preserving whole words by never cutting a word in half.
/// If a complete word (plus the delimiter, if any) cannot fit, then only the delimiter is returned.
/// When truncating from the left, the delimiter is prepended if a complete word can be preserved;
/// otherwise, only the delimiter is returned.
/// The allowed count is computed by counting only letters/digits.
public string? Truncate(string? value, int totalLength, string? delimiter, TruncateFrom truncateFrom = TruncateFrom.Right)
// Treat a null delimiter as an empty string.
// If the delimiter itself is longer than totalLength, fallback to a plain substring.
// Count all alphanumeric characters. If they already fit, return full string.

reasons.detail: Complex alphanumeric-counting plus word-boundary backtracking has off-by-one candidateIndex logic, inconsistent delimiter vs totalLength handling, and commented-out guards that cause wrong prefix/suffix or delimiter-only returns.

diff.text: // If the delimiter itself is longer than totalLength, fallback to a plain substring.
// Count all alphanumeric characters. If they already fit, return full string.
static string TruncateRight(string value, int totalLength, string delimiter)
// Allowed alphanumeric count from the beginning.

reasons.detail: Off-by-one in TruncateRight/Left when alphaCount==totalLength sets candidateIndex=i not i+1, truncating the last fitting char and breaking word-boundary backtrack (e.g. 'Hello' with limit 5 returns 'Hell').

diff.text: // If the candidate index is in the middle of a word, backtrack to last whitespace.

reasons.detail: Two break conditions use inconsistent boundaries (i+1 vs i) and the alphaCount==totalLength branch ignores delimiter length, causing off-by-one truncation and totalLength violations on right-truncate.

diff.text: // If the candidate index is in the middle of a word, backtrack to last whitespace.
return delimiter; // no complete word fits
// Get the substring and trim trailing spaces.
// Ensure the final length does not exceed totalLength.

reasons.detail: Marked region returns only delimiter when prefix alphanumeric count plus delimiter exceeds totalLength and uses TrimEnd plus letter/digit-only length check, which discards a valid whole-word prefix that fits the documented alphanumeric limit and hides the off-by-one candidateIndex (i vs i+1) from the preceding loop.

diff.text: static string TruncateLeft(string value, int totalLength, string delimiter)

reasons.detail: Marked return cascade mixes alphanumeric-only prefixLength with raw delimiter.Length against totalLength, so when delimiter fits budget but prefix+delimiter exceeds it the code returns only delimiter instead of trimming/backtracking, and the delimiter>totalLength branches return prefix/empty inconsistently with the spec's 'only delimiter' rule.

diff.text: // If candidateIndex is in the middle of a word, move forward to the next whitespace.

reasons.detail: Left-truncation loop uses alphaCount+dLen==totalLength vs alphaCount==totalLength inconsistently and nextSpace is overwritten to the leftmost whitespace, so candidateIndex can include extra non-alphanumerics or snap to the wrong word boundary and exceed/violates the documented alphanumeric budget.

diff.text: // If candidateIndex is in the middle of a word, move forward to the next whitespace.

prs.title: Tweaks to the Wondrous calendar system
prs.taskSummary:
Tweaks to the Wondrous calendar system

- Remove WondrousYearInfo: we never need both parts together,
  so just use two separate methods instead.
- Remove the cache: a dictionary is going to be more involved
  than the simple array lookup anyway, and it's not thread-safe.
- Simplify CalculateStartOfYearDays - aside from anything else,
  now we don't need to use DateTime :)
- Change WondrousYearMonthDayCalculator to *only* use the
  "Ayyam-i-Ha are part of month 18" model, e.g. for GetDaysInMonth.
  The alternative model of "Ayyam-i-Ha are in month 0" is used
  extensively in WondrousCalendarSy

diff.text: private const int WondrousMaxYear = 1000; // current lookup tables are pre-calculated for a thousand years
///     There are 19 months in a year. Between the 18th and 19th month are the "days of Ha" (Ayyam-i-Ha).
///     - treat Ayyam-i-Ha as month 0. This will cause problems if 0 is treated as unknown. When stored internally,
///       NodaTime months are converted to 0-based numbers, so this would by -1 which is not supported.
///     - treat Ayyam-i-Ha as month -1. This would be a problem if the base classes convert to 0 based months
///     - treat Ayyam-i-Ha as month 19. This is confusing because the 19th month would be displayed as month #20.
///     - treat Ayyam-i-Ha as month 20. This will cause problems if months are sorted naively.
///     - treat Ayyam-i-Ha as extra days in month 18. This would require special handling to sometimes display
///       days in "month 18" as being Ayyam-i-Ha, but we have no direct control over display.
/// This version will treat Ayyam-i-Ha days as extra days in month 18.

diff.text: These types can act like generic notification listeners, that fire when something in the DOM changes. They would be also used internally by nodes, which may need to know when their content changes. As an example: The `HtmlStyleElement` needs to know when its content changes, since the new content has to be parsed and evaluated.

A `MutationObserver` reports *what* changed, allocates a record per mutation and delivers asynchronously. When the question is only *whether* anything changed - invalidating a cache over a live collection, for instance - `Document.MutationVersion` answers it without any of that. It is advanced synchronously with the mutation itself, costs a single increment, and covers the parser's own construction of the tree as well as the DOM APIs, so two equal readings mean nothing in the document changed in between. Compare two readings for equality; the value itself is opaque. It is declared on `Document` rather than on `IDocument`, so reaching it means a cast: `((Document)document).MutationVersion`.

prs.title: Read Liquid words and lenient tag syntax like Shopify (#1142)
prs.taskSummary:
Read Liquid words and lenient tag syntax like Shopify (#1142)

* Match Liquid words at word boundaries

Liquid words (operators, tag arguments and tag names matched in place) were
matched with Terms.Text, which accepts any prefix: `{% for i inp %}` looped
over `p`, `{% if a orb %}` read `a or b`, and `{% elsewhere %}` was an `else`.

A word now ends where no letter, digit or `_` follows it, like `\w` in
Shopify's regular expressions. The check is in one helper, `Word`, so it can
be swapped for Parlot's Keyword once its boundary is configurable. A `-` ends a
word, so trim markers (`{%else-%}`)

diff.text: Shopify Liquid ignores some content and reads some words in ways that can be surprising. Fluid does the same:

- Operators made of letters, like `contains`, `or` and `and`, and the other words of the syntax, like `with` or `else`, end where no letter, digit or `_` follows them: `{% if a contains"b" %}` is valid, `{% if a orb %}` is an error instead of `a or b`, and `{% render 'card' format: 'short' %}` passes a `format` argument.
- The `in` of a `for` or `tablerow` tag is followed by whitespace: `{% for i in(1..3) %}` is invalid.
- A tag name is made of letters, digits and `_`, so `{% comment-x %}` is a `comment` tag, and `{% my-tag %}` is the `my` tag.
- Tags without arguments ignore anything after their name: closing tags, `else`, `comment`, `raw`, `break`, `continue` and `ifchanged`, as in `{% endfor items %}`.

- In a `for` tag, `reversed` is only read right after the collection, even when it starts a longer word: `{% for i in items reversedx %}` is reversed, `{% for i in items limit: 2 reversed %}` is not. A `tablerow` tag ignores it.
- The `limit`, `offset` and `cols` attributes are read anywhere after the collection, and anything else is ignored: `{% for i in items foo, limit: 2 %}` renders two items.
Liquid follows strict rules with regard to whitespace support. By default, all spaces and new lines are preserved from the template.

A frame here has a document rather than a context to navigate, so the three answers were to move the page (the wrong document), do nothing, or refuse — and **doing nothing is the one that must not be chosen**: against a silent no-op `event-global-is-still-set-when-coercing-beforeunload-result.html` waits forever for the frame's `load` and the whole file times out, where a refusal fails it fast. Reads answer the frame's own URL and not the page's, which is why `location` is shadowed rather than inherited; `assign`, `replace` and `reload` are absent, which is loud the same way |

| a frame served `application/xhtml+xml` | HTML [reads it with the XML parser](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-lifecycle.html#read-xml), as it does every XML MIME type | the default content-type mapping sends it to the **HTML** parser, so `<foo>x</foo>` comes back as an HTML document with the text inside an `<html><body>` skeleton. `text/xml` and `application/xml` are right once `WithXml()` is registered; `image/svg+xml` produces no document at all. **Unreachable from this side**, and measured rather than assumed: `DefaultDocumentFactory.Register`/`Unregister` are public, but the configuration *adds* services rather than replacing them, so a second `IDocumentFactory` breaks AngleSharp's own `Single()` resolution for every page — and removing the first (`Without<IDocumentFactory>()`) discards whatever `WithXml()` contributed, which regresses `text/xml` and `application/xml` to HTML. AngleSharp.Xml's XML creator is not public, so nothing can be composed in its place without this package building documents itself. The same package answers the type correctly through `DOMParser` (`Dom/Views/JsDomParser`), which routes all four XML types to `XmlParser` — so a frame and `parseFromString` disagree about the same bytes. `NeedsXmlDocuments` in the browser lane, and 195 rows of `Document-createElementNS.html` plus 49 of `Document-createElement.html` |

Clamping to the intrinsic size would put a second geometry beside the one `getBoundingClientRect`, `elementFromPoint`, `DOM.getBoxModel` and `offsetX` all answer from, and the two would disagree about the same click; the coordinate is honestly the box's instead. `Events/ActivationBehaviors` selects it and `Runtime/FormSubmitter` submits it |

diff.text: # AngleSharp divergences found by the DOM bindings
**Data, not instructions.** This is the register [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) points at: every place AngleSharp
answers differently from the standard that the bindings had to work around, so the next agent recognises one
it has already met and nobody patches around the same thing twice. The rule that governs it — record the
divergence, never work around it silently, never open an issue on AngleSharp without being asked — is in that
file, which is where an agent is told to look before it edits anything here.
Divergences that are **AngleSharp's**, found by this work and to be reported upstream rather than patched

| `node.isConnected` | DOM §4.4: whether the node's shadow-including root is a document | `INode` has no member for it at all, so nothing is projected — and every client library asks a node handle this before it clicks it, so an absent member makes every element read as detached. Re-declared in `additions` |
| `delete el.dataset.foo` | DOM §3.5's deleter removes the content attribute | `IStringMap.Remove` sets its value to `null` and leaves `data-foo` in place |
| `el.querySelectorAll(…)` | DOM §4.2.6 returns a static `NodeList` | returns an `IHtmlCollection<IElement>`, so `Object.prototype.toString` reports `[object HTMLCollection]` |
| `el.style.color` | CSSOM serializes an opaque colour as `rgb(r, g, b)` | serializes every colour as `rgba(r, g, b, 1)` |
| `el.children === el.children` | one `HTMLCollection` per element | a fresh collection per call, so the wrapper cache has nothing to key identity on |
| `el.id` when the attribute is absent | `""` | `null`, which is why the conversion table's default is the empty string |
| `insertAdjacentHTML`'s position | a WebIDL enumeration | `AdjacentPosition` carries no `[DomLiterals]`; the lower-case-field heuristic is what catches it |

| `matchMedia(q).matches` | evaluates the query against the viewport | `CssMediaQueryList.ComputeMatched` is `return false`, so **every** query answers `false` — a page asking whether it is on a narrow screen is always told no. `Runtime/MediaQuery` answers the subset a page branches on instead |
| `document.currentScript` | HTML §4.12.1: the script whose text is running | the head of the *deferred* script queue, so it is `null` for exactly the case a page uses it in |

| `document.readyState` | HTML §3.1.6: the host advances it and fires `readystatechange` | `Document.ReadyState`'s setter is `protected`, so nothing outside AngleSharp can move it; a host driving its own parse has to shadow the member. `Runtime/PageRuntime.ReadyState` is that shadow |

| `<script async src>` | HTML: it executes the moment its fetch lands, in no particular order | `HtmlScriptElement.InvokeLoadingScript` puts `defer` and `async` into the one `_loadingScripts` queue, so an async script executes in document order at the end of the parse |

| `document.write` after the parse | HTML: it implies `document.open()`, which replaces the document | `Document.Open` blocks on `PromptToUnloadAsync().Result` and `Unload(recycle: true).Wait()` — synchronous waits on asynchronous work, inside a DOM member a script calls. `DomHostHooks.Write` refuses instead |

| a custom `IResourceLoader` | a host wants scripts and style sheets and not images | every request processor asks the same `IResourceLoader`, and only `WithDefaultLoader`'s `LoaderOptions` can filter by kind — so a host supplying its own loader has to refuse per element type itself |

| `location.host = …` (and `pathname`, `port`, `protocol`, `search`) | a navigation the page can observe | raises `Location.Changed`, which `Document.LocationChanged` handles in a fire-and-forget `async void` calling `IBrowsingContext.OpenAsync` — on whatever thread the setter ran on. **Unreachable from script**, because `Runtime/LocationInstaller` shadows every `Location` member with an own property over the page's own URL; AngleSharp's location is never written |

| `el.classList.add('x')` | DOM §7.1's token list writes the content attribute, which is an attribute change | `TokenList` writes it through its own `Changed` event, which raises neither `IAttributeObserver.NotifyChange` nor a mutation record, so an observed `class` attribute reported no `attributeChangedCallback`. **No longer reachable**: §7.1's update steps are `DomTokenListMembers`' and are a plain *set an attribute value* — the same door `setAttribute` comes through — so the notification arrives. The row stays because the AngleSharp behaviour is unchanged and any other caller of `ITokenList` still meets it |

| `el.setAttributeNS(ns, 'x', 'v')` | an attribute change like any other | `IAttributeObserver` is not called for a namespaced write, so only a *connected* element's change is seen — through the mutation record instead |
| `attr.value = 'v'` on an `Attr` node | DOM §4.9.2: setting an attribute's value is a change of that attribute | neither channel is raised, so nothing observes it |

| `<th>` and `<td>` | HTML gives both `HTMLTableCellElement` | `IHtmlTableHeaderCellElement` and `IHtmlTableDataCellElement`, two `[DomName]` interfaces HTML does not have, which is why the `HTMLElement` constructor's interface check accepts an ancestor — `CustomElements/CustomElementRegistry.Construction.cs` states what that relaxation costs |

| `observer.disconnect()` | DOM §4.3.3 empties the observer's registered-node list | `MutationObserver.Disconnect` unregisters it from the document but leaves that list populated, so the **next** `observe()` of any node silently re-registers every node it used to watch |

| `observer.observe(document, …)` | observes the document node | `Connect` silently retargets a `Document` to its `documentElement`, so a `childList` mutation of the document itself is never reported. With `subtree: true` — how nearly every page writes it — nothing else changes |

| `observe(…)` with bad options | a `TypeError` | a `DomException` (`TypeMismatchError` / `SyntaxError`), and its resolution of the dictionary's optional members differs from the standard's: `{ attributeOldValue: false }` alone is valid in DOM and invalid there |
| `record.addedNodes` on an attribute record | an empty `NodeList` | `null`, for both `Added` and `Removed` |
| `IShadowRoot.Mode` | `ShadowRoot.mode` | the one member of the interface with no `[DomName]`, so nothing says it is projected |
| `slot.assignedNodes()` | DOM §4.2.5 | named `getDistributedNodes`, the Shadow DOM v0 spelling |

| `getComputedStyle(span).display` | `inline` | the empty string: the cascade reports only what a stylesheet *declared*, and `display: inline` is CSS's initial value, so the user-agent sheet does not declare it. A declared one (`div` → `block`) resolves. `Dom/Views/ResolvedStyle` answers the initial value over it for this and nine other properties, which is the whole of the exception — see [`../AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md)'s divergence table |

| the computed style is writable | CSSOM's computed flag makes every write a `NoModificationAllowedError` | an ordinary writable declaration, and a detached one, so a write neither throws nor changes anything readable — see `Dom/Views/ReadOnlyStyleDeclaration` |

| `el.click()` on a checkbox, radio, `<summary>` or `<a href>` | the element's activation behaviour runs | `DoClick` dispatches on AngleSharp's own bus and runs **no activation behaviour at all**, with or without a browsing context: nothing toggles, opens or navigates |
| `document.activeElement` | the focused element, or the body | `null` for the life of every document — nothing in AngleSharp ever assigns it, `DoFocus()` included |
| `el.tabIndex` when the attribute is absent | −1 for anything not inherently focusable | 0 for every element, including a bare `<div>`, so it cannot decide focusability |
| `input.labels` | the `<label>`s whose `for` names the control | an empty collection |

| `label.control` | the labeled control: the `for` target, or the first labelable **descendant** | `null` for a control the label contains, which is the commoner spelling; `Events/ActivationBehaviors` computes it instead so a click inside a wrapping label reaches its checkbox |
| `script.src` | HTML reflects it *as a URL*, so it answers the resolved absolute URL | the raw attribute value, so `<script src="a.js">.src` is `"a.js"` where a browser answers `"http://…/a.js"` |
| `select.selectedIndex` with no `selected` option | 0 — the selectedness-setting algorithm picks the first option of a non-`multiple`, display-size-1 select | −1 |
| `input.value = …` | the cursor moves to the end and the selection is dropped | `SelectionStart`/`SelectionEnd` are left where they were, so they can point past the end of the new value |
| `input.setSelectionRange` on a `type=checkbox` | `InvalidStateError` — the type does not support selection | answers, so the type test has to be the caller's |

| `DomException.Name` | DOM's error name — `HierarchyRequestError` | the **enum field name**, `HierarchyRequest`, so the string can never be handed to a page; `DomFailures.NameOf` is the table that maps a `DomError` to the standard's name, and `DomExceptionTests` pins every row of it |

| `DomError.Validation` | WebIDL's legacy code for `ValidationError` is 16 | 15 — the value of `DomError.InvalidAccess` — so the two are one number and no `ValidationError` can be told from an `InvalidAccessError` |

| a `DomException`'s message | a browser names the operation and what it refused | AngleSharp's own sentence, which is what `DomFailures` puts after the `Failed to execute '<interface>.<member>': ` prefix. DOM specifies a `name` and nothing about wording, and a page branches on the name |

| `insertAdjacentHTML('beforebegin')` on an element with no parent element | HTML step 2: a `NoModificationAllowedError` | the one `DomException` in the assembly built from a *string*, so it carries no `DomError` at all and its `Name` is the sentence "The element has no parent."; `DomHostHooks.InsertAdjacentHtml` makes that refusal itself |

| `createElementNS(null, 'a:b')`, `setAttributeNS(null, 'a:b', …)` | DOM's validate-and-extract is a `NamespaceError` for a prefixed name with no namespace | no refusal at all, so an element or attribute is created with a prefix nothing declares. The `xmlns` half of the same algorithm *is* checked |

| `walker.previousNode()` | DOM §6.1: a walk that ends, because every pass moves the node strictly backward in pre-order or returns | `TreeWalker.ToPrevious` never assigns the `sibling` variable inside the loop that reads it and never climbs to the parent, so it **spins forever** the moment the previous sibling is not accepted outright — a `FILTER_REJECT`, a `FILTER_SKIP`, or a `currentNode` outside the root beside a node `whatToShow` excludes. **The one algorithm this package does not take from AngleSharp**: `Dom/Views/DomTreeWalker` implements all seven traversals, because carrying only the broken method would leave two walks and a termination argument for neither. It is a denial of service rather than a conformance gap — a node `whatToShow` excludes is `FILTER_SKIP` without the page's filter being called, so the loop never re-enters the engine and no constraint, cancellation token or page budget is ever consulted ([#3765](https://github.com/sebastienros/jint/issues/3765)) |

| `el.classList.add('')` / `add('a b')` | DOM §7.1: a `SyntaxError` for the empty token, an `InvalidCharacterError` for one containing ASCII whitespace | neither is validated, so `ITokenList` takes both. **The whole of §7.1's mutating half is `Dom/Collections/DomTokenListMembers` now**, because the validation steps are only the first of five things the interface cannot say: `toggle`'s `force` is a CLR `bool force = false`, which cannot tell "given as false" from "not given"; there is no `replace` and no `supports`; the indexer throws where WebIDL's indexed getter answers `null`; and the *update steps* rewrite the attribute in serialized form even when the token set did not move, where AngleSharp notifies only on a change. What stays AngleSharp's is the token set itself and the attribute it is bound to |

| `iframe.sandbox.supports('allow-scripts')` | HTML defines a supported-token set for `rel` and `sandbox`, so this is `true` | there is no supported-token set anywhere in the assembly, so `supports` answers the `TypeError` DOM prescribes for an attribute that defines none — right for `class`, and a refusal for the two attributes that do define one |

| `iframe.sandbox instanceof DOMTokenList` | DOM merged `DOMSettableTokenList` into `DOMTokenList` in 2016 | `ISettableTokenList` still carries `[DomName("DOMSettableTokenList")]`, so `sandbox`, `htmlFor` and `link.sizes` land on an interface the standard no longer has. Its one member *is* skipped — `Value` answers the serialized token set where DOM's `value` is the attribute verbatim — so the shape is empty and everything is inherited; the name is the whole of what is left |

| `node.replaceWith(…)` | DOM §4.2.7's name | `IChildNode` is `[DomName("replace")]`, a name the standard has not got — skipped and re-declared. The algorithm diverges twice more: it converts its arguments before it checks for a parent, so a parentless child's call still moves them; and it refuses when the child is among its own replacements |

| `parent.replaceChildren(…)` | DOM §4.2.6 | absent, and **deliberately so**: replace-all is one mutation record, `ReplaceChild` with a fragment records the removal and no addition, and `ParentNode-replaceChildren.html` waits for that record — so the member turns a document that reports into one that times out |
| `el.setAttributeNode(a)` on an observed attribute | the reaction's `newValue` is the attribute's | `null`: an `Attr` write reaches the attribute observer without its value |

| `doc instanceof XMLDocument` | DOM §4.5 gives an XML document its own interface | one `XmlDocument` serves an XML parse *and* `new Document()`, which DOM makes a plain `Document`, so the CLR type cannot decide it: `HTMLFrameSetElement`'s shape with no local name to select on |

| `input.selectionDirection` on a control nothing has selected in | HTML [§4.10.5.4](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#dom-textarea-input-selectiondirection): `none`, and `setSelectionRange(start, end)` with no third argument sets `none` | `forward` in both cases, so a page cannot tell a selection a user dragged left-to-right from one that has no direction at all. `Events/TextEditing` compares which end the caret is at rather than the string, which is its own model of direction anyway; without that, the first caret key in every control would look like a change of direction and fire a `selectionchange` |

| `el.classList.add('')` / `add('a b')` | DOM §7.1: a `SyntaxError` for the empty token, an `InvalidCharacterError` for one containing ASCII whitespace | neither is validated, so the token list takes both |

| `el.classList.add('')` / `add('a b')` | DOM §7.1: a `SyntaxError` for the empty token, an `InvalidCharacterError` for one containing ASCII whitespace | neither is validated, so `ITokenList` takes both. **§7.1's mutating half is `Dom/Collections/DomTokenListMembers` now**: validation is the first of five things the interface cannot say, with `toggle`'s `bool force = false` (which cannot tell "given as false" from "not given"), no `replace`, no `supports`, an indexer that throws where WebIDL answers `null`, and update steps that rewrite the attribute even when the set did not move. The token set and its attribute stay AngleSharp's |

diff.text: /// The <c>Element</c> and <c>Node</c> members the DOM standard requires and AngleSharp has no
/// <c>[DomName]</c> for, so nothing could generate them.
/// Every one of them is a member on the shortest path of an ordinary page — a client library that
/// feature-detects <c>toggleAttribute</c> takes a slower path when it is missing and one that does not
/// throws — and each fails the same way before a test can say anything about behaviour:
/// <c>Property '…' of object is not a function</c>.
/// None of them re-implements anything. The Attr-node family is AngleSharp's
/// INamedNodeMap, which has every one of the five under WebIDL's other spelling
/// switch over <c>InsertBefore</c> and <c>AppendChild</c>. What is here is the standard's spelling and the
/// Legacy — <c>===</c> answers it, and the wrapper cache makes <c>===</c> reliable — but normative, and
internal static JsValue IsSameNode(INode target, JsValue[] arguments)
internal static JsValue HasAttributes(IElement target) => DomConvert.Bool(target.Attributes.Length != 0);
/// <remarks>The qualified names, in the attribute list's own order, which is the order the parser made.</remarks>
internal static JsValue GetAttributeNames(DomRealm realm, IElement target)
internal static JsValue ToggleAttribute(IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
// Step 2: an HTML element in the HTML namespace lower-cases the name, which is the same fold
// setAttribute makes and the reason `toggleAttribute("FOO")` and `hasAttribute("foo")` agree.
if (target is IHtmlElement && string.Equals(target.NamespaceUri, NamespaceNames.HtmlUri, StringComparison.Ordinal))
// Step 4: the value is the empty string, so a boolean content attribute reads as present.
internal static JsValue GetAttributeNode(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
internal static JsValue GetAttributeNodeNS(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
internal static JsValue SetAttributeNode(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
internal static JsValue SetAttributeNodeNS(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
/// DOM removes the attribute node rather than a name: an Attr the element does not hold
/// is a <c>NotFoundError</c>, which is why this compares the map's own entry by identity rather than
/// handing the name to <c>RemoveNamedItem</c> and trusting it.
internal static JsValue RemoveAttributeNode(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
"The node provided is not an attribute of this element.");
internal static JsValue InsertAdjacentElement(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
return realm.WrapNodeValue(InsertAdjacent(realm, target, where, node, Member));
/// The one member outside the exclusion table: upstream's own testharness result renderer calls it, and
/// its absence is why the browser lane's <c>testharnessreport.js</c> turns that renderer off.
internal static JsValue InsertAdjacentText(DomRealm realm, IElement target, JsValue[] arguments)
/// https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#insert-adjacent — the four positions, ASCII case-insensitively, and a
/// <c>beforebegin</c> and <c>afterend</c> answer <see langword="null"/> for an element with no parent
/// rather than refusing, which is where this differs from <c>insertAdjacentHTML</c>'s
private static INode? InsertAdjacent(DomRealm realm, IElement target, string where, INode node, string member)
"The value provided ('" + where + "') is not one of 'beforeBegin', 'afterBegin', 'beforeEnd', or 'afterEnd'.");
/// The <c>Node</c> and <c>Element</c> members the DOM standard requires and AngleSharp has no
/// <c>[DomName]</c> for — <c>Dom/DomElementMembers</c> — plus the two whose only fault was their name.
// DOM §4.2.7 spells it `replaceWith`; AngleSharp's IChildNode carries [DomName("replace")], so the
// mixin projected a name the standard does not have.
// The new attribute's value is the empty string, and `force` decides in both directions.
// DOM §4.9 removes an attribute *node*, so one that belongs elsewhere is a refusal rather than a
// silent miss on a name that happens to match.
try { e.insertAdjacentElement('somewhere', document.createElement('u')) } catch (err) { return err.name }
// Case-insensitive, which is what a page written against the original IE spelling relies on.
.Should().Be("|", "an element with no parent has nowhere to put a sibling, so both answer null");
// The alias is a member of its own, not the same function object: WebIDL declares two operations.
"(() => { try { document.body.webkitMatchesSelector('[') } catch (e) { return e.name } return 'no throw' })()")
.Should().Be("SyntaxError", "the alias refuses a bad selector the way matches does");

diff.text: **A polyfill must match the downlevel API's *behaviour*, not just its signature.** `Polyfills.Order` is a hand-written merge sort rather than a call to `OrderBy` because LINQ's sort on .NET Framework is a quicksort with no depth limit and no fallback, so an inconsistent comparer — which a JavaScript comparison function is allowed to be — makes it spin forever instead of terminating. Sorting and searching are where downlevel implementations differ most; check them rather than assuming the older framework's version is merely slower.

**Number parsing is the other one, and it is not a polyfill at all — it replaces the BCL everywhere.** .NET Framework's `double.Parse` is not IEEE correctly-rounded: it lands one ULP off for about one in sixty-five 18-digit operands, fails rather than saturating to an infinity on overflow, loses the sign of `-0`, and rejects a leading `+` under the styles the spec lanes passed it. ECMA-262 makes every string-to-number conversion one rounding to the nearest Number, so the answer may not depend on which target framework an embedder loaded — and `parseFloat`, `Number(…)` and `JSON.parse` disagreed with each other on `net472` for the same digits (sebastienros/jint#3532). `NumberParser.TryParseDouble` reads the digits itself and is the only route any of them, or `TemporalHelpers`, takes to a `double`. Two things about it are deliberate. It is **unconditional** rather than `#if !NET8_0_OR_GREATER`: the `netstandard` assets can be loaded on any runtime, so a guard would still have to compile the managed parser for them, and running it everywhere is what puts it under the whole test262 suite instead of only under the `net472` test leg. And it is **exact rather than approximately right** — a `ulong` fast path and a Clinger scaling by an exactly-representable power of ten settle the common shapes in one rounding, and everything else goes through `BigInteger` division against the rounding boundary. A "close enough" decimal parser is the failure mode here; `Jint.Tests/Runtime/StringToNumberPrecisionTests.cs` holds it to an exact oracle on every target framework.

A real member always beats an extension member, so on the frameworks that *do* have the API the BCL implementation is what binds — usually the better one (`double.IsFinite` is a single exponent-bits test where the polyfill is two calls). There is no ambiguity to resolve, and nothing to undo when a target framework is eventually dropped: delete the guarded block and every call site is already correct.

This matters beyond tidiness. Spec algorithms are phrased in terms like "if *x* is finite", so a call site reading `double.IsFinite(x)` can be checked against the spec text at a glance where `!double.IsNaN(x) && !double.IsInfinity(x)` has to be decoded first. `Polyfills.cs` is the single home for these — `string.Join(char, …)` and the `ReadOnlySpan<char>` `Parse`/`TryParse` overloads are already there. Add to it rather than working around it.
